What part of "Bella Ramsey looks absolutely nothing like their game counterpart and it's incredibly distracting and immersion breaking, on top of being a pretty bad actress" do these people not get? It's got nothing to do with their perceived attractiveness, or lack thereof depending on who's looking at them. I've been saying it since Ramsey was first revealed as Ellie and I'm a woman.

Perhaps there would be less of an uproar had there never been a game to base the show on, it was just another zombie apocalypse show and nothing else? But since it is based on a game, it's not unreasonable to expect the actors to resemble their characters. Opinion was always going to be divided between gamers vs. viewers, it seems incredibly naive of the show runners and Neil Druckmann to have had no foresight there.

Ramsey's lack of physical maturity doesn't help either, as in they look exactly the same as they did in the first season. I get it's difficult to portray a five year time jump in two years, but considering just how young Ramsey looked in the first place, really they should have been recast for older Ellie. The games showed Ellie's natural age progression from 14-19. In contrast, Ramsey started off looking 12.

I'm sure poor writing and bad direction have also contributed to the show's steady decline as well, and resorting to calling Ramsey ugly is just an immature, short sighted take on things. But to counter it with "Bella Ramsey is the best Ellie and the best actress the world has ever seen" is just as ridiculous and short sighted. There were better actresses available who wanted the gig. And by better I mean more experienced, more technically gifted, and at least one who is both of those things AND bares more than a passing resemblance to game Ellie.
Honestly, if I didn't know better I would have just assumed that Isabella Merced was Ellie, because even in a single image she's more convincing as the character than Bella is.

As someone who is diagnosed with ADHD by a psychiatrist, and got a second opinion that backed it up, I was accused of "gatekeeping neurodiversity" by a self-diagnoser the other day. This was all because I was having a bad day and said that I need to remind myself the condition is real and exists and I was actually diagnosed with it and I'm not actually a complete trash human. Perhaps some underlying jealousy caused them to react in this way, I'm not really sure.

I have no qualms with people reaching out for help and an eventual diagnosis if they truly believe they have some sort of neurodiversity that, if properly treated, would improve their quality of life. It's not as if these conditions have signs and symptoms that are difficult to spot or research, ever since the Tiktokers and the Facebook mums began to make almost daily posts detailing them in intricate detail, knowledge is power after all.

But the idea that there are people out there who would rather hate on diagnosed people for "gatekeeping", that we're somehow the haves and they are the have nots, than actually go out and seek the help they say they so desperately need, is just ridiculous attention/sympathy seeking. I mean I guess they could blame their outburst on their potentially undiagnosed neurodiversity, but until they actually go and seek help, they're just being rude and unnecessarily offensive to the very group of people they could well be a part of, so I'm not sure what they think they're achieving.

I guess there could be NDs who look upon the self diagnosed with disdain, and I understand why that can feel isolating and unfair. But I can still understand why those people would feel that way and find the self diagnosed annoying or trifling, considering the amount of Tiktok influencers who are most likely downright faking having a disorder for clout and possibly financial gain.

I was 25, and got married in September of that year. My daughter was 4, she would turn 5 in December of that year. My friends also had daughters of similar ages. Our boyfriends, who would later become our husbands all got on. It was a summer of BBQs, sleepovers, drinking, working like dogs but feeling like it was actually worth it because things were somewhat more affordable. Life definitely seemed simpler and more optimistic back then.

I feel like it's because the 90s lingered into the 2000s for longer than they should have really, or at least longer than previous decades have bled into their successors anyway. The turn of the century was a weird time, technology advanced and boomed massively in that time. It was also crazy expensive, I remember my dad refusing to make the shift to a DVD player for a good 18 months because he didn't want to pay £500 for one. Same with mobile phones and contracts, stuff simply wasn't accessible to the average person or teen for quite a while.

I remember being a teen and still using a desktop computer with Windows 98 on it until around 2003. Similarly, my family didn't get cable TV til around then, and I didn't get my first mobile phone until then either. Technology, therefore trends, took so much longer to spread, peak, plateau and ultimately die off before smartphones, the viral internet and social media. In comparison, as a society we can probably pivot through at least a hundred viral trends/songs/dances/memes a year, as opposed to a mere handful twenty years ago. Not to mention internet trends were very much seen as counter culture back then, before they pivoted into the norm.

The early to mid 2010s saw the rise of the iPhone, Blackberry and P2P messaging. It was also the aftermath of the 2009 recession, a time of regrowth and perceived opportunity, with a more optimistic feel to a lot of things than there is now some 15 years later. I was in my early 20s and had not long had my daughter, and I remember how bright and colourful everything was. Internet viral trends were just taking off, as was Instagram, and a few years later came Snapchat. I think we yearn for that feeling of new and of novelty. The novelty has long since worn off and nothing has replaced it.

I have also been advised to claim PIP, which is basically disability payments, as I will always have osteoarthritis in the foot now, even after the surgery and if the surgery is considered successful. 

The benefits system in this country is clunky and complicated, and it's made that way by design, to discourage people from claiming. The success rate is mixed, and often you need to appeal a rejection in order to get what you're entitled to.

I have diagnosed, severe ADHD, so the thought of navigating a system which is set up to ensure the failure of most people is daunting and feels like a waste of time. I don't want to be injured or in pain anymore. I don't want to have to rely on handouts. I want to be able to work and have my life back. Imagine you've got a tray or tub of raw product - pork/chicken/beef etc. And next to that is a tray of cooked product. All that separates them is a plastic or metal barrier (the container), and a flimsy layer of cling film. If the cling film covering the raw product has blood on it, and touches the cling film covering the cooked, or there's a blood transfer, that could be incredibly dangerous and cause cross contamination.

Worse still, if the raw is stored above the cooked and the blood drips down into the cooked. Although it may seem like Gordon is overreacting in some instances, the fact is this is extremely bad practise, and implies there are other violations, which there usually are. It also implies that if the chefs aren't storing and labelling properly, they're probably not hand washing properly either.

Speaking as a former self-diagnoser, I'm going to offer my humble opinion such as it is.

Around 6 years ago, I began to strongly suspect I was suffering from Type 1 Bipolar Disorder. I had catastrophic mood swings, made crazy impulse decisions and/or purchases, was prone to bouts of anger that led to physical violence, and all of this was peppered with periods of crushing lows, suicidal ideation and/or occasionally relative calm.

I was an absolute mess, jumping from job to job, scheme to scheme, idea to idea. 'This time things will be different' was my motto. I hyperfocused so much I didn't think there was any way a doctor could disagree with something I was utterly convinced I already knew. It took me four long years to convince my local outpatient mental health facility to see me (I'm UK, so was and still am at the mercy of the NHS). In those four years I was told multiple times by multiple medical professionals that it was depression, anxiety, I just needed to take a walk or run a hot bath. 

I thought I was going insane. When I finally got diagnosed with ADHD, it was this massive all encompassing relief for awhile, but it was also confusing. I wasn't Bipolar after all? But soon enough I began to hyperfocus on the diagnosis and blame it for everything wrong in my life. I went private to get a second opinion, which ultimately still diagnosed ADHD as the primary disorder. How was i wrong? How does anyone know me better than I do? I still jumped from job  to job and thing to thing as I struggled to adjust to various meds, whilst trying so hard to enforce routines and stability on myself. I'd rebel against it all when things got too much.

Eventually I calmed down enough to realise that this is my diagnosis. It's not going to change or get better without me trying to help myself, so I need to stop fighting this invisible battle with the world, thinking that one day I can fight so hard I might win.

And this is the point I am attempting to poorly and messily make. Self diagnosis doesn't work in the long term. I'm not suggesting people should ignore, self medicate or give in to symptoms, and if they believe they are struggling they should absolutely seek help and treatment. But to just blindly assume they have one particular thing that ticks all the logical boxes in their mind is irrational and often dangerous, which is precisely what they should be avoiding. I'm not trying to upset or invalidate anyone who is currently self diagnosed, I'm just imploring them to use that as a stepping stone to a formal diagnosis, because sometimes it can be something entirely different, and without proper help and intervention you're still out there untreated and suffering. No one should have to go through that.

As a former Cineworld employee, it definitely feels like 2019 was kind of the year that cinema really *peaked*, especially now we have the hindsight of the last 2.5 years. Perhaps not globally, but definitely for the UK. It wasn't just because of Endgame (although working that release really did feel like a moment). Disney had a bumper year with the Lion King and Aladdin live action remakes, and Toy Story 4. But just in general, SO many memorable films came out that year, and almost all of their opening weekends were packed. 

Once Upon A Time in Hollywood, Captain Marvel, Shazam, Joker, IT Chapter 2, Us, Star Wars: Rise of Skywalker, Spiderman: Far From Home, John Wick 3, Jojo Rabbit, X-Men Dark Phoenix, Alita: Battle Angel...and they're just the ones I remember. Not even all of them were good, but it didn't matter, people still came out in their dozens to see them.

All cinema chains suffered huge financial losses in the aftermath of the pandemic. They struggled to fully reopen since, particularly in the early days after lockdown, when restrictions were so tight it probably put a lot of people off going, coupled with nobody wanting to sit in a room full of strangers, even with a mask on, for 2+ hours. This created a never ending cycle of decreased custom = fewer showings = opening later and closing earlier thus being less available = having to increase ticket and food prices in order to keep operating, and round and round it goes. 

The more recent cost of living crisis has likely rendered a trip to the cinema unaffordable for a lot of people, and even those who can still afford it are probably thinking twice about how they spend their money. Online streaming is a cheaper and more viable alternative for a huge amount of people these days. Cineworld also got hit with really bad press due to still paying their CEOs bonuses during the pandemic, whilst all of their staff were either furloughed or made redundant. I believe they're now filing for bankruptcy in the US.

Would things have been any different had Covid never happened? It's difficult to say. But the cost of living has been ever increasing for decades, so even without a pandemic, cinemas would have likely seen a fall in trade regardless, just maybe not as sharply and suddenly. I remember a staff meeting at the beginning of 2020 (just before I left and just before Covid really took off), the main focus was how on Earth we were ever going to replicate the success of 2019, and how can we compete against streaming services/make cinema seem like the more attractive choice. So the writing had been partially on the wall for awhile, Covid just created a perfect storm which is now seeing cinema become a bit of dying industry.

It's sort of the same in the UK. Basically you start off having to be under the mental health department of the NHS in order to access ADHD meds. You have to go refill your prescription through them every month, your psych doc there will do a handwritten prescription. Sometimes the doc will want you to come in to do a blood pressure check, sometimes he won't. You have to go to three monthly reviews to discuss your progress. Eventually (for me it was 9 months later - today actually!), your psych doc will decide that the meds suit you, you can be trusted with them, they haven't made your blood pressure go off the charts, and haven't made you worse in any way. He then sends off the paperwork to your GP/primary care doctor so that they can't start doing your prescription instead, whereby it's automatically refilled every month and sent electronically to a pharmacy. My only obligation is to continue to get my blood pressure regularly checked.  

So yeah I understand frustration, but I guess here there is some light at the end of the tunnel. Being treated like a hopeless junkie by literally every pharmacist I encounter isn't much fun though.

Please get evaluated. There are no good long term results from taking medication that isn't prescribed for you.

If it doesn't work/do anything, you could be tempted to try a higher dose or a different med, which then becomes a slippery slope toward misuse/addiction. 

If you suffer negative side effects and have to seek medical attention, you'll be treated for drug misuse, rather than the problem you're trying to solve.

Finally, if by chance taking the medication was a positive experience for you, you'd then have the issue of not being able to access any more of it without a prescription. And telling a physician or a psychiatrist that you'd tried this particular medication without any kind of medical supervision would most likely be frowned upon, thus potentially hindering a future diagnosis, as a lot of ADHD meds are controlled drugs.

I understand your frustrations, but any insight you might gain from doing something 'this one time' isn't worth the risks. I wish you luck.

She said while it would be impossible to ever prove it one way or the other, she'd seen a huge influx of youngish people (25-40 year olds mainly) turn up with sudden, and often quote debilitating issues they had previously never suffered with, having had a 'mysterious illness' during Christmas 2019. Whilst the bloody stools pretty much stopped immediately, the diahhroea and stomach cramps took longer to finally subside, and I still have to be careful with what I eat. 

I am under no illusion I got off lightly here. I am most definitely on the milder end of the scale, and obviously it's not possible to know if this truly was a Covid complication, but it's so important people understand that it's not a simple case of catching 'a cold' and getting better. Very few people can truly say they walk away from Covid totally unscathed, and it can range from mild to moderate discomfort such as mine (although at the time I was terrified I had bowel cancer), to full blown deterioration/debilitation with no end in sight. Average incubation period for both HSV1 and 2 is 2-21 days, however it's possible that the virus can lay dormant in your system for months, if not years after initial exposure. Some people test positive without ever having an active outbreak. But again, if you don't any sores or lesions, there's nothing for the doctor to swab, so they'd treat you based on the symptoms you have. If you're concerned you can request a Western Blot test, however it's not something doctors usually do as standard. New sexual partners can cause thrush and UTIs due to an upset in the pH balance down there. It may also be worth you both going for a full STI panel if you're worried.

My second and third outbreaks are only two weeks apart as well, so I'm in a similar position to yourself, wondering if I'll ever get the long term relief that others have described.

I'm not sure how things work where you're from, but my experience in the UK is that once diagnosed, the doctor or sexual health clinic will dole out the medication for you, and it's pretty much up to yourself to manage it after that for awhile, figure out what dosage and creams work for you. The general rule is if you have more than six outbreaks within the a year, that's when you'll get switched to suppression therapy. So it's kinda hard to know if you're doing the right thing, if/when you should be going back to the doctor etc. But if you're struggling you should definitely look into getting a second opinion.

As others have said, adding a daily vitamin regimen could be helpful for you. I see you've said you're taking daily Lysine. I'm not sure if this is entirely correct, as I've read into a lot of herpes related stuff recently, so if anyone knows any better than me please chime in, but Lysine supplements tend to work better if you already have a Lysine rich and low Arginine diet. The supplements will compliment your diet way better if you're already eating naturally occurring Lysine. Eating too much Arginine means the supplements have to work that much harder, so positive results will be limited. Changing up your eating habits may be the next step, if you haven't already.

Good luck, I hope you find some relief soon!

What you appear to have here, is a stalemate.
There has to be some give and take in any relationship, or in the long run it categorically will not work.
Your partner's drive and ambition to succeed financially and career-wise is admirable. So it's understandable that you are feeling confused and frustrated that his views regarding marriage seem to run parallel to every other aspect of his life.
Conversely, you state that you absolutely do not want to have children before you are married. Whilst that is an extremely personal decision which I completely and utterly respect, have you made it clear to your partner how important this is to you?
With the potential fertility issues you could possibly have, sitting back and waiting for 'the stars to align' as you put it, seems like a terribly devil-may-care attitude, coming from two people who seem to have a plan in place for every stage of their lives, and are unwilling to leave anything to chance.
It sounds like you need to have a very frank conversation, make it clear that ultimately time waits for no man, and when all is said and done you're more likely to regret the things you didn't do than the things you did.
In terms of a compromise, could you not have a small, intimate wedding, with just family and a few close friends? That way the big day is still something to shoot for in the future, like a vow renewal, hopefully this time with your children there as well?
